To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the probability of retiring because of mandatory retirement decreased between 1994 (when 7% of respondents retired because of mandatory retirement) and 2002 (when 5.7% of respondents did so) due to a change in the workforce composition that made it less likely that respondents would be forced to retire, while the expected age of respondents at retirement increased by 3.7 years, with that increase due to changes in the workforce composition and the preferences and constraints that respondents faced.

between 1994-2002 there was a 1.4 percentage point increase in the probability that a worker will retire at the mandatory retirement age (with a substantial part of that increase due to changes in the composition of workers and the other part due to changes in preferences and constraints) and a 3.6 year increase in the age of retirement (with the entire increase being due to changes in preference and constraints).

between 1994 and the 2002, there was an increase in the expected retirement age and the probability of mandatory retirement, the former almost exclusively and the latter mostly due to preference and constraint changes."
In summary, our research is concerned with

the impact of changes in the composition of workers and changes in workers' preferences and constraints on two important labour market outcomes, namely the expected age of labour force withdrawal and the probability of retiring involuntarily due to mandatory retirement.
the impact of mandatory retirement on the labour supply of older Canadians and the impact of mandatory retire-ment on the age structure of the labour force.
the determinants of the probability and expected age of retirement and the changes in these outcomes that have taken place between 1994 to 2002.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the probability of retiring at age 55-64 has decreased and the expected age at retirement has increased between 1994-2002.
the probability of retiring because of a mandatory retirement policy has not changed much between 1994-2002, while the expected age of mandatory retirement has increased by 3.7 years.
mandatory retirement has become less important as a determinant of the age of retirement and that the age of retirement has increased.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, while there are some important changes in the composition of workers that may have an impact on retirement, the changes in the preferences of the workforce and the constraints that they face appear to be the most important factors influencing retirement.

, while there are some changes in the determinants of retirement due to mandatory retirement between 1994-2002, the most important change is that, in the absence of a change in the age of eligibility for the Canada Pension Plan (CPP) and Quebec Pension Plan (QPP), the expected age of mandatory retirement has increased by about 4 years.

, in the absence of a change in the law, employers should not expect to be able to increase the proportion of employees who retire due to mandatory retirement in the near future and that the expected age at which people retire will continue to rise in Canada.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the expected age of mandatory retirement has increased substantially over the past decade.
the retirement experience of the baby-boomer cohort is not necessarily the same as that of their parents.
there has been an important shift in the preferences and/or constraints of workers that has increased the expected age of workers' retirement and decreased the expected age of mandatory retirement.
